Description: Every custom SwiftUI view must conform to View and implement a body property. Keep body focused on layout; extract sub-views for logic or reuse.
Do: Return a single top-level container from body; use @ViewBuilder for conditional or multi-branch returns.
Don't: Put business logic or data transformation directly inside body — it re-runs on every render pass.
Code Good: struct ProfileView: View { var body: some View { Text(user.name) } }
Code Bad: struct ProfileView: View { var body: some View { let _ = loadData(); Text(name) } }

Description: SwiftUI redraws only the views whose inputs changed. Extracting independent sub-views limits the redraw scope and improves performance.
Do: Break large body trees into smaller named View structs with their own parameters.
Don't: Build one mega-body with nested VStack closures hundreds of lines long.
Code Good: struct AvatarView: View { let url: URL; var body: some View { AsyncImage(url: url) } }
Code Bad: // 300-line body with all layout inline

Description: Annotate helper methods or computed properties that return multiple conditional branches with @ViewBuilder so SwiftUI can handle the resulting opaque types.
Do: Use @ViewBuilder on functions that contain if/switch branching returning different View types.
Don't: Return AnyType-erased views (AnyView) for branching — erases diffing identity and hurts performance.
Code Good: @ViewBuilder var badge: some View { if isPro { ProBadge() } else { FreeBadge() } }
Code Bad: var badge: some View { return AnyView(isPro ? ProBadge() : FreeBadge()) }

Guideline: Prefer value types for view data
Description: SwiftUI views are structs (value types). Pass immutable value-type data directly to view initialisers to keep rendering deterministic and thread-safe.
Do: Pass lightweight value-type structs to views; use @Binding only when the child needs write-back.
Don't: Pass reference-type objects directly into view initialisers without using @StateObject or @ObservedObject.
Code Good: struct ItemRow: View { let item: Item }
Code Bad: struct ItemRow: View { var item: ItemObject } // reference type, ownership unclear

Description: Use @State for private view-owned values that SwiftUI should observe and redraw on change. It should never leak outside the view.
Do: Prefix @State properties with private; initialise with a literal default value.
Don't: Use @State for data that is shared between multiple views or that comes from a model layer.
Code Bad: @State var sharedCart: [Item] = [] // should be in a model

Description: Pass @Binding when a child view needs to mutate a piece of state owned by a parent. It creates a two-way reference without transferring ownership.
Do: Create Binding in the parent and pass with $ prefix; child declares @Binding var.
Don't: Use @State in child when it receives a value from a parent that the parent also needs to observe.
Code Bad: // child has @State var isOn copying parent value

Description: Use the @Observable macro instead of ObservableObject + @Published for model objects in iOS 17+. It provides fine-grained property tracking with less boilerplate.
Do: Annotate model classes with @Observable; access with @State or direct property in View.
Don't: Use @ObservableObject with @Published for new code targeting iOS 17+ — the older pattern is less efficient.
Code Bad: class CartModel: ObservableObject { @Published var items: [Item] = [] } // legacy

Description: Use @StateObject when a view is responsible for creating and owning an ObservableObject. SwiftUI initialises it once and keeps it alive across redraws.
Do: Declare @StateObject in the view that creates the model; pass to children via @ObservedObject or environment.
Don't: Use @ObservedObject for a model the view creates — it re-initialises on every redraw.
Code Bad: @ObservedObject var vm = CartViewModel() // recreated on redraw

Description: Read system-provided values (colorScheme, locale, sizeCategory, dismiss) from the environment using @Environment with a typed key path.
Do: Use @Environment(\.dismiss) or @Environment(\.openURL) for system actions instead of custom callbacks.
Don't: Pass dismiss or open-URL callbacks manually through view hierarchies — the environment is the canonical channel.
Code Bad: // passing dismiss: () -> Void through 4 view layers

Description: Use @EnvironmentObject to inject a shared ObservableObject into a deep sub-tree without passing it through every intermediate view.
Do: Inject at the highest ancestor that needs the object using .environmentObject(); consume only where required.
Don't: Inject @EnvironmentObject at the root for every model — prefer @Observable or explicit init for locally scoped data.
Code Bad: // passing AuthSession through 8 struct inits

Description: Define custom EnvironmentKey and EnvironmentValues extension to propagate design tokens (spacing scale and brand colour) through the tree without prop drilling.
Do: Create a typed EnvironmentKey with a default value; expose via a convenience extension on EnvironmentValues.
Don't: Pass design tokens as explicit parameters to every leaf widget.
Code Bad: struct LeafView: View { let brandColor: Color }

Description: Pass an explicit alignment argument to stacks. Default leading/top alignment is often wrong for internationalised layouts; use .center or .leading explicitly.
Do: Always specify alignment and spacing in stack initialisers for predictable layout across locales.
Don't: Rely on default implicit stack alignment and discover layout bugs only on RTL devices.
Code Bad: VStack { ... } // implicit alignment

Description: Use LazyVStack inside ScrollView for lists that have more items than fit on screen. Lazy stacks only build views for visible items.
Do: Pair LazyVStack with a ForEach and ensure each item view is cheap to initialise.
Don't: Use VStack inside ScrollView for long dynamic lists — all children are created upfront.
Code Bad: ScrollView { VStack { ForEach(items) { ItemRow($0) } } }

Description: Use the Grid container (iOS 16+) for two-dimensional table-like layouts instead of nested HStack/VStack which cannot align columns across rows.
Do: Use GridRow inside Grid; use .gridColumnAlignment for per-column alignment.
Don't: Nest multiple HStacks inside a VStack to simulate a grid — column alignment is impossible.
Code Bad: VStack { HStack { Text("Name"); Text("Score") } }

Description: Use ViewThatFits to present the first view whose ideal size fits in the available space. Ideal for adaptive buttons or text that should truncate gracefully.
Do: Provide views in descending complexity order inside ViewThatFits — the first fitting view is rendered.
Don't: Use GeometryReader to manually measure and switch layouts — ViewThatFits is safer and declarative.
Code Bad: GeometryReader { geo in geo.size.width > 300 ? WideButtonLabel() : CompactButtonLabel() }

Description: Use NavigationStack (iOS 16+) instead of the deprecated NavigationView. It supports programmatic navigation via a NavigationPath.
Do: Initialise NavigationStack with a path binding for programmatic push/pop; use .navigationDestination for typed values.
Don't: Use NavigationView in new code — it is deprecated and does not support typed deep links.
Code Bad: NavigationView { List { NavigationLink(...) } } // deprecated

Description: Use NavigationPath to hold a type-erased list of pushed values. Serialise it for scene restoration and universal link handling.
Do: Store NavigationPath in @StateObject or @SceneStorage; append typed values to navigate programmatically.
Don't: Maintain a parallel array of pushed routes manually outside of NavigationPath.
Code Bad: @State var stack: [Item] = [] // manual stack, loses type safety

Description: Register destinations for value types using .navigationDestination(for:destination:). This decouples navigation links from their destinations and enables programmatic navigation.
Do: Declare .navigationDestination once in the NavigationStack root; keep it close to the stack declaration.
Don't: Embed NavigationLink(destination:) with an explicit view instance — it eagerly creates the destination.
Code Good: List { ForEach(items) { NavigationLink(value: $0) { Text($0.title) } } }.navigationDestination(for: Item.self) { ItemDetail($0) }
Code Bad: NavigationLink(destination: ItemDetail(item)) { Text(item.title) } // eager init

Description: Attach .task to a view to run async work scoped to the view's lifetime. SwiftUI cancels the task automatically when the view disappears.
Do: Use .task { await vm.load() } instead of onAppear + Task { } patterns to get automatic cancellation.
Don't: Use onAppear with a detached Task — the task outlives the view and may update deallocated state.
Code Bad: .onAppear { Task { await viewModel.fetchProducts() } }

Description: Create expensive objects (networking clients and databases) with @StateObject so they live for exactly the view's lifetime — no longer, no shorter.
Do: Pair @StateObject with a class conforming to @Observable or ObservableObject; deinitialise resources in deinit.
Don't: Instantiate services or clients inside @ObservedObject — they are recreated on every redraw.
Code Bad: @ObservedObject var store = ProductStore() // recreated each render

Description: Conform value-type view inputs to Equatable so SwiftUI can skip redrawing when inputs have not changed.
Do: Add Equatable to model structs and use EquatableView wrapper for views with expensive body computation.
Don't: Pass non-Equatable objects that always look different to SwiftUI's differ — forces constant redraws.
Code Good: struct ItemView: View & Equatable { let item: Item }
Code Bad: struct ItemView: View { let item: ItemClass } // reference, always differs

Description: SwiftUI calls body frequently. Any synchronous heavy work blocks the main thread and causes dropped frames. Move computation to async tasks or pre-calculated properties.
Do: Precompute derived data in the model or in .task; expose a simple ready-to-render value to the view.
Don't: Filter/sort large arrays or format dates inside body — it runs on every frame.
Code Bad: Text(items.filter{$0.active}.map{$0.price}.reduce(0,+).formatted())

Description: Wrap state mutations inside withAnimation to animate all resulting layout and property changes declaratively.
Do: Pass a custom Animation curve (spring and easeInOut) to withAnimation for natural feel; use transaction for one-off overrides.
Don't: Apply implicit .animation(.default) on container views — it propagates to every sub-view unintentionally.
Code Bad: // .animation(.default) on VStack animates all children

Description: Use the value-bound .animation(_:value:) modifier to tie an animation to a specific value change instead of the deprecated unbounded .animation().
Do: Always provide the value parameter so the animation fires only when that specific value changes.
Don't: Use the deprecated .animation(.spring()) without a value — it triggers on every property change of the view.
Code Bad: .animation(.easeOut) // deprecated, fires on all changes

Description: Use matchedGeometryEffect with a shared namespace to animate a view element between two visual states (list to detail hero image).
Do: Apply the same id and namespace to both source and destination views inside a matched geometry pair.
Don't: Manually offset/scale a view to simulate a hero transition — matchedGeometryEffect handles frame interpolation automatically.
Code Bad: // manual frame calculation for hero animation

Description: Every interactive or informational custom view that does not have an inherent semantic label needs an explicit .accessibilityLabel so VoiceOver can announce it.
Do: Provide a concise noun-phrase label describing the element's purpose; use .accessibilityHint for action description.
Don't: Expose an unlabelled icon button — VoiceOver reads the SF Symbol name which is meaningless to users.
Code Bad: Image(systemName: "heart") // VoiceOver says heart

Description: Use SwiftUI's built-in Text and system fonts which automatically scale with the user's preferred text size. Test at all accessibility sizes.
Do: Use .font(.body) or named styles; wrap fixed-width containers in ViewThatFits to handle large text sizes.
Don't: Set a fixed font size with .font(.system(size: 14)) — it ignores the user's accessibility text size setting.
Code Bad: Text(title).font(.system(size: 14)) // ignores Dynamic Type

Description: Mark purely decorative images and views with .accessibilityHidden(true) so VoiceOver skips them and reduces noise for screen reader users.
Do: Apply .accessibilityHidden(true) to dividers, background gradients and icon decorations that duplicate adjacent label text.
Don't: Leave decorative images without an accessibility annotation — VoiceOver will attempt to read their file name.
Code Bad: Image("banner-bg") // VoiceOver reads file name
